Name: language_distance_interference_map
Title: The Interference Ledger: Mapping When Knowledge in One Language Corrupts Answers in Another Across Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Prior work shows knowledge is stored language-specifically while reasoning is shared. We hypothesize that this language-specific storage produces measurable, directional cross-lingual interference: injecting a false fact in language A will corrupt answers to the same question in typologically/script-close languages far more than distant ones, and this interference footprint is causally localized to a small set of shared 'concept-binding' neurons in mid layers. No existing work has built a controlled causal map linking language distance to knowledge interference (as opposed to transfer).
Related Work: Recent work characterizes cross-lingual knowledge transfer (ECLeKTic, Hu et al. 2024) and shows knowledge is stored separately per language while reasoning shares neurons. Riemenschneider & Frank (2025) trace concept neurons converging across languages; Dong et al. (2025) find privacy-universal vs language-specific neurons. All these study transfer, alignment, or leakage. None study interference: whether editing/inserting knowledge in one language actively degrades correctness in others, and how this negative transfer scales with language distance. Our proposal flips the lens from 'does knowledge transfer help?' to 'when does cross-lingual entanglement hurt?', combining controlled fact-injection (in-context and via knowledge editing like ROME/MEMIT) with a distance-graded causal neuron analysis. This directional-interference causal map is novel.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs are known to store factual knowledge in largely language-specific subspaces while sharing abstract reasoning circuitry. A neglected consequence is interference: because concepts are partially bound in a shared mid-layer space, knowledge asserted in one language may spill over and corrupt answers in others. We introduce the Interference Ledger, a controlled framework to quantify directional cross-lingual knowledge interference as a function of language distance. Using paired factual questions across a diverse set of languages spanning scripts and typological families, we inject counterfactual statements (via both in-context prompting and localized knowledge editing) in a single source language and measure induced error rates on the identical question in all target languages. We predict interference decays with typological and script distance, is asymmetric (high-resource sources contaminate more), and is causally mediated by a compact set of shared concept-binding neurons in intermediate layers. We test the causal claim by ablating and steering these neurons, expecting to selectively suppress interference while preserving legitimate transfer. Deliverables include: (1) a reusable multilingual counterfactual-interference benchmark, (2) a quantitative interference-vs-distance model, (3) a causal localization of interference-carrying neurons, and (4) a training-free intervention that reduces harmful spillover. This reframes multilingual entanglement as a controllable safety and reliability axis, complementing existing transfer-focused analyses.
Experiments: 1) Benchmark construction: Take ~500 factual QA items (subject-relation-object triples) from Wikidata, create parallel questions in ~10 languages spanning close/far distances to English (e.g., German, French, Spanish, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili, Turkish) using template-based generation + native-speaker/MT verification. 2) Baseline accuracy: measure per-language closed-book accuracy on open-source models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B). 3) In-context interference: prepend a counterfactual assertion (wrong object) in source language L_s, then query the same fact in every target language L_t; compute Interference Rate = fraction of previously-correct answers flipped to the injected wrong answer or to error. Build an N-language x N-language directional interference matrix. 4) Knowledge-editing interference: apply ROME/MEMIT to edit a fact using only L_s data, then measure flip rate across L_t; compare to in-context results. 5) Distance modeling: regress interference on typological distance (lang2vec/URIEL features), script overlap (binary/shared-token overlap), embedding similarity, and resource level; report correlations and an interpretable predictive model. 6) Test asymmetry: compare L_s->L_t vs L_t->L_s interference. 7) Causal localization: use activation patching and logit-lens to identify mid-layer neurons/directions whose activation mediates the interference; validate by ablation. 8) Mitigation: apply a training-free steering/ablation on identified neurons; measure reduction in harmful interference vs retention of beneficial transfer (using ECLeKTic-style transfer items). Metrics: Interference Rate, distance-correlation (Spearman), asymmetry index, transfer retention, and net reliability gain.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Template-generated multilingual questions may contain translation artifacts; mitigated via native/MT verification and filtering. 2) Interference effects may be small or noisy for well-known facts; we control by selecting facts the model initially answers correctly. 3) Knowledge editing methods (ROME/MEMIT) are best-tuned for English/decoder models and may edit imperfectly in other languages, confounding causal claims; we cross-validate with in-context injection. 4) Causal neuron localization can be fragile across models; we report robustness across multiple models and use activation patching as the gold standard. 5) Distance metrics (URIEL) are imperfect proxies; we triangulate with script and embedding-based distances.
